topic: Blog share: burnout recovery, why rest is not the whole answer
text:
A week off is the usual advice for burnout. Then the first Monday back arrives, and it can feel like you never left.

In our new blog, Matthew Hallam looks at why rest alone often falls short. The World Health Organization describes burnout as the result of chronic workplace stress that has not been well managed, and Australia's model code of practice asks workplaces to manage psychosocial hazards such as high demands, low control and poor support.

Research in healthy workers adds a useful detail: wellbeing rises during a holiday and eases back in the weeks after returning to work. None of those studies looked at people with burnout, and none tested a single week off, but the pattern is worth knowing.

For clinicians, it shifts the question at review from "did you rest enough?" to "what did you go back to?"

Read the blog: https://equalpsychology.com.au/blog/burnout-recovery-why-rest-is-not-the-whole-answer

Key sources:
World Health Organization. (2019). Burn-out an "occupational phenomenon": International Classification of Diseases. https://www.who.int/news-room/detail/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases
Safe Work Australia. (2022). Model Code of Practice: Managing psychosocial hazards at work. https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-08/model_code_of_practice_-_managing_psychosocial_hazards_at_work_25082022_0.pdf
Grant, R. S., Buchanan, B. E., & Shockley, K. M. (2025). I need a vacation: A meta-analysis of vacation and employee well-being. Journal of Applied Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/apl0001262
